challenges.reason: Ogle concerns a former cohabitant's assertion that she was a tenant entitled to unlawful-eviction protections after the homeowner excluded her. The court examined whether a rental agreement or tenancy existed and concluded the record supported only social-guest status.
challenges.sourcePassage: Appellant's unlawful-eviction argument was premised on her asserted status as a tenant rather than a social guest. The court stated: "There is no evidence in the record that the parties entered into a rental agreement of any sort or that either of them considered her a tenant in the home."

challenges.reason: Pyle sets out the requirement that IIED conduct be extreme and outrageous, beyond all possible bounds of decency, and utterly intolerable in a civilized community. Thus, it supports the cited outrageous-conduct standard relevant to denial of an IIED claim.
challenges.sourcePassage: "In order to recover on an action for intentional infliction of serious emotional stress four elements must be proved," including "that the actor's conduct was so extreme and outrageous as to go 'beyond all possible bounds of decency' and was such that it can be considered as 'utterly intolerable in a civilized community.'"

challenges.reason: Ogle v. Disbrow is correctly identified and concerns a resident’s claim of unlawful/self-help eviction after the homeowner excluded her. The court addressed whether she was a tenant or merely a social guest and held the record did not support tenant status.
challenges.sourcePassage: "Appellant also asserts she set forth a cause of action for unlawful eviction. This argument is premised on appellant's belief that she possessed status as a tenant, not a social guest, while living with appellee.... There is no evidence in the record that the parties entered into a rental agreement of any sort or that either of them considered her a tenant in the home."

challenges.reason: Pyle addresses an intentional-infliction-of-emotional-distress claim and states that actionable conduct must be extreme and outrageous—going beyond all possible bounds of decency and utterly intolerable in a civilized community. The source also states that the appellate court determined the trial court’s judgment on the claim was against the manifest weight of the evidence.
challenges.sourcePassage: "In order to recover on an action for intentional infliction of serious emotional stress four elements must be proved: ... that the actor’s conduct was so extreme and outrageous as to go ‘beyond all possible bounds of decency’ and was such that it can be considered as ‘utterly intolerable in a civilized community[.]’" The opinion further states: "In light of our determination, explained below, that the decision of the trial court is against the manifest weight of the evidence, these three assignments of error will be addressed as one."

challenges.reason: The cited case is Lorain Natl. Bank v. Saratoga Apts., reported at 61 Ohio App.3d 127. It expressly states that an appellate court reviewing summary judgment applies the same standard as the trial court, which supports the stated de novo-review proposition. The supplied source has no reliable reporter-page boundaries for measuring the pinpoint to page 129.

challenges.sourcePassage: "In reviewing a summary judgment, the lower court and the appellate court utilize the same standard, i.e., we review the judgment independently and without deference to the trial court’s determination."
